whatTheyArgued: Emotion arises when a tendency to respond is arrested or inhibited. Music sets up expectations from learned stylistic norms; 'embodied meaning' is one musical event pointing to and making us expect another, as opposed to designative reference to extramusical things (via Huron's notes on Meyer; I did not read the book).

scholarship.ref: David Huron, 'Notes on Meyer: Emotion and Meaning in Music', ch. 1 (reading notes by a leading music cognition scholar)
scholarship.supports: tendency/inhibition thesis; expected progression as norm and deviation from it; embodied vs designative meaning
scholarship.disputes: critics say Meyer over-weights expectation as the source of meaning, is culture-bound (unfamiliar styles seem to carry little meaning) and favours conscious processing

scholarship.ref: Lorraine, 'Music, tendencies, and inhibitions: reflections on a theory of Leonard Meyer' (PhilPapers record only; abstract not read)
scholarship.supports: existence of philosophical critique of the tendency/inhibition account

bends.ours: 'Deviation from what was learned is where meaning arises.'
bends.theirs: Meaning for Meyer is expectation-based in general (fulfilment, delay and violation all carry it); emotion specifically comes from inhibition. 'Deviation = meaning' flattens that, and it was about music in a learned style, not about arbitrary arriving data.
